subject: Banking
title: Can Regulation Actually Work?
description: A 60-second lesson on Can Regulation Actually Work?.

hook.text: Banks are regulated by dozens of agencies worldwide. Yet scandals keep happening.

buildup.text: US banks face oversight from the Fed, OCC, FDIC, SEC, CFPB, and state regulators.

discovery.text: Regulators earn $80-150K. Bank compliance lawyers earn $500K+.

twist.text: The revolving door — regulators leaving to work at banks they oversaw — creates conflicts of interest at every level.

climax.text: Regulation fails when regulators are outspent, outtalented, and eventually hired by the banks they regulate.

punchline.text: Dozens of agencies. Outspent and outtalented. Then hired by the banks.

quiz.question: What is the 'revolving door' problem in banking regulation?
options: Regulators leaving to work for the banks they previously oversaw

details.summary: Despite decades of banking regulation and billions spent on compliance, scandals keep recurring, raising the fundamental question of whether rules can ever truly prevent misconduct in profit-driven institutions.
details.whyItMatters: If regulation cannot prevent banking misconduct, society must consider alternative approaches like structural reform, cultural change, or stronger personal liability for executives.
takeaways: Regulations typically follow scandals rather than preventing them
Banks spend over $270 billion annually on compliance globally
Enforcement gaps and regulatory capture undermine even good rules

faq.question: Why do banking scandals keep happening despite regulation?
faq.answer: Profit incentives often outweigh penalty risks. Banks calculate that fines cost less than the money made from misconduct. Regulators are also frequently outmatched by bank resources and political lobbying.

faq.question: What would make banking regulation more effective?
faq.answer: Stronger personal criminal liability for executives, higher fines relative to profits, better-paid regulators, and structural separation of risky activities from deposit-taking are commonly proposed reforms.
